confirmed: Read the complete 104241-character markdown conversion, including references and Appendices A-E; independently checked the relevant PDF pages and extracted Table 2 with pymupdf.find_tables().
source.version is correct: arXiv:2310.08433v1, dated 12 Oct 2023 on the p. 1 side stamp; the local PDF has 25 pages, including appendices. The document title and both author names also match p. 1.

S1.design_class = ai_vs_human, eligibility.context_class = ai_vs_human, and eligibility.core = no are supported: models and human writers produced stories separately, and writers were instructed not to use LLMs (PDF pp. 3-6, Sections 3.1-3.4). No randomized people study is reported anywhere in the document.
participants.n_analyzed = 5 correctly counts the human writers. There are 60 LLM stories plus 5 human stories and 10 student raters; no count of people randomized is reported (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4).

The 12 models, their listed versions/sizes, and Bing Creative mode match Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 3-4). Each model supplied 5 stories from a fresh-state prompt; human writers were suggested 250 to 1200 words, and model stories averaged 379 words (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4).

The rubric has 10 items scored out of 10, with an overall total out of 100. The raters were Honours/postgraduate Creative Writing students with experience applying the scale, and authorship was blinded (PDF pp. 5-6, Table 1 and Section 3.4).
S1-O1 reported means and SDs match Table 2 exactly: GPT-4 80.2±7.3, human 70.1±17.4, Claude 74.4±15.9, and the bottom-row average 56.6±15.8 (PDF p. 6).

For overall scores, the unequal-variance two-tailed t-test does not distinguish humans from the top 6 models at α = 0.05; the bottom 6 are worse. The separate individual-metric analysis uses n = 100 and reports p = 0.00031 for GPT-4 versus humans; that is not a people count or the overall-score test (PDF p. 7, Section 4.2).

S1-O2 item 5 values match Table 2: human 8.0±2, GPT-4 7.6±1, Claude 7.1±2.3, Bing 7.0±1.6, average 5.2±2. The authors cannot reject equal originality for those three models versus humans; the other models score significantly lower (PDF p. 6, Table 2; pp. 7-8, Section 4.4).

S1-O3 item 10 values match Table 2: GPT-4 6.0±2.8, human 6.4±3.4, Claude 6.5±2.5, Bing 6.2±2.6, average 3.4±2.2. Section 4.3 reports a two-tailed test at α = 0.05 separating the other models from humans and these three LLMs, without a GPT-4-versus-human humor test result (PDF pp. 6-7).

S1-O4 item 7 values match Table 2: GPT-4 8.1±1.4, human 4.9±2.1, GPT-3.5 6.8±1.5, average 5.5±2.3. Both ChatGPT versions significantly exceed humans at α = 0.05; six other model means are higher without a detected significant difference (PDF p. 6, Table 2; p. 8, Section 4.5).

The one_line_finding accurately reproduces the overall and creativity means/SDs and the nonsignificant creativity comparison. The higher overall mean is descriptive; the overall-score t-test is also nonsignificant (PDF p. 6, Table 2; pp. 7-8, Sections 4.2 and 4.4).
Appendix E supplies six selected stories and their rater scores in Tables 4-9 (PDF pp. 19-25; tables on pp. 20, 21, 22, 24, 25). These are examples from the same corpus, not additional studies.
This is an original output-comparison study, not a synthesis; leaving synthesis counts and pooled estimates empty is appropriate (PDF pp. 3-9, Sections 3-6).
summary: The AI-versus-human classification, five-writer count, source version, and reported results are supported; there is no randomized AI-assistance study. Seven corrections address missing assignment/eligibility codes, an unprinted derived rating total, an appendix locator, and the omitted data link.
